English: IoT devices are ordinary objects with an internet connection: cameras, TVs, speakers, watches, plugs, doorbells, baby monitors. OT systems control physical processes: a society's water pump, a rooftop solar inverter, a lift, a fire alarm. Both are computers, but they are rarely treated as computers — so they are rarely updated or secured.

Most smart-device attacks need no special skill. Lists of default usernames and passwords are public, and automated programs scan the internet for devices that still use them. In 2016, the Mirai botnet took over hundreds of thousands of cameras and video recorders with default passwords and used them to knock major websites offline.
If a device came with a password printed on a sticker, change it the day you install it.
Securing the home or shop router

The router is the front door of every device behind it. Two passwords matter: the Wi-Fi password that devices use to join, and the admin password that opens the router's settings page. Many routers supplied by internet providers still use a default admin password.

Cameras protect homes and shops — and, if hijacked, expose them. A secure camera has a changed password, current firmware, MFA on its app and no unnecessary remote access. A respectful camera covers only what it needs to, never private spaces of others, and people know it is there. Under the DPDP Act 2023, video of identifiable people is personal data.

A housing society installed eight cameras with an online viewing app and left the installer's default password. A resident's teenage son found the live feed listed on a website of exposed cameras. The committee changed all passwords, updated the recorder's firmware, removed public cloud sharing, moved one camera that overlooked a flat's balcony, and put up a notice.

Smart speakers listen for a wake word; smart TVs record viewing habits; fitness bands record routes and health data; children's watches share location. Each has privacy settings that are rarely changed. Small Bluetooth trackers, meant for finding keys, can be misused to follow a person; modern phones can alert you to an unknown tracker travelling with you.
If an unknown tracker is found

Safety first: a tracker placed on someone may be part of stalking or domestic abuse. Note and photograph it and the phone alert; do not go home if the person feels unsafe; contact the police or 181. Disabling it may alert the person who placed it, so plan with the person and the police (Module 7).

Smart-device incidents combine privacy, safety and evidence. Preserve first (screenshots of the app, the leaked page address, the tracker alert), then isolate and secure — and check every other device on the same network, because one weak device usually means others.
